chunks: Swiss cheesing a plane. The question: What is "swiss cheesing" a plane?
Swiss cheesing is slang for a plane that has so many clearance holes around its vias (plated holes) that it looks like Swiss cheese.
It happens under chips with dense via fields, and it is worst when holes line up in rows.
The copper between holes becomes thin necks, so resistance and inductance (opposition to steady and to fast-changing current) go up.
A row of merged holes also acts as a slot, which makes signal return currents detour and increases crosstalk (noise leaking between traces) and radiation.
Think of the perforated line between postage stamps. A straight row of small holes makes a weak line that tears. That is a slot.
Scattered, offset holes would leave the paper in one piece. Aligned via holes make the same weak line for current.
Left: antipads spaced at their own diameter touch along each row and merge into slots.
Right: holes of the same size, spread wider and offset from row to row, leave continuous copper channels (this layout also has fewer vias per unit area, which is part of why it works).
Antipad: the clearance hole in a plane around a via that does not connect to it. Slot: a long gap in a plane, made when holes in a row merge.
Web: the copper strip left between two neighboring holes. It is the pitch minus the hole diameter.
Return current: the current flowing back to its source, usually in the plane under the signal trace. Stagger: offsetting rows of vias so the holes do not line up.
Say vias sit 1. 0 mm apart and each antipad is 0. 9 mm wide. The web between them is only 1. 0 - 0. 9 = 0. 1 mm. A row of those is almost a slot.
Staggering the rows at the same via density, about one via per mm², raises the nearest spacing to about 1. 07 mm, so the narrowest web grows only to about 0. 17 mm.
The real gain is that no straight slot remains. To widen the webs, shrink the antipads: 0. 7 mm antipads leave 0. 3 mm.
That is the whole idea: align and pack holes carelessly and you cut the plane into strips.
"Swiss cheesing is a plane so perforated by via antipads that it looks like Swiss cheese, typically under BGAs when via rows align.
The copper between holes becomes narrow necks, raising resistance and inductance and creating slots that break return paths, so crosstalk and EMI worsen.
I stagger vias, shrink antipads, leave copper bridges, and use fewer or blind vias."
